analysis.one_liner: Makes illegal robocalling a crime and doubles penalties for faking caller ID.
analysis.headline: The bill to criminalize illegal robocalls was introduced in the Senate with four sponsors and referred to committee, where it has not advanced.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill adds criminal penalties to the existing law against unwanted robocalls and robotexts. A person who knowingly and willfully breaks the rules could face up to a year in prison, and up to three years for large-scale operations, repeat offenders, calls meant to further a felony, or calls that cost victims $5,000 or more [S2]. It also doubles the civil fine for deliberately sending inaccurate caller ID information, from $10,000 to $20,000 per violation, making it harder and more expensive for scammers to hide behind fake numbers [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who receive illegal robocalls and robotexts, especially seniors and others targeted by phone scams. Today the main penalty is civil fines, which the Federal Communications Commission and state enforcers must pursue; the bill would let the Justice Department prosecute the worst robocall operators as criminals, adding prison time as a deterrent [S2]. The fines for falsifying caller ID double, which raises the cost of the spoofed numbers scammers use to trick people into answering [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Adds a new criminal penalty: anyone who willfully and knowingly violates the robocall rules faces up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both [S2].

Raises the maximum to 3 years for aggravated cases: repeat offenders, operations exceeding 100,000 calls in a day (or 1 million in a month, or 10 million in a year), calls intended to further a felony, or offenses causing victims $5,000 or more in losses [S2].
Doubles the penalty for providing inaccurate caller identification information from $10,000 to $20,000, targeting the spoofing tactic scammers use to make calls look local or legitimate [S2].
The definition of a 'call' covers autodialed texts sent without the recipient's prior consent, so robotext spam falls under the same penalties [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If enacted, the cost falls on robocall operations and telemarketers who break the law, including the criminal enterprises behind phone scams, plus legitimate callers who willfully flout consent rules. The Justice Department would bear the cost of new prosecutions.

drawbacks.text: Criminal penalties apply only to willful and knowing violations, so the bill does not create criminal liability for good-faith mistakes by legitimate callers [S2].
The bill adds enforcement tools but does not change the underlying rules, so it does nothing by itself to reduce call volume; it depends on federal prosecutors deciding to bring cases [S2].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that criminal prosecution is slow and resource-intensive, and that the bill's practical effect depends on Justice Department priorities rather than the statute alone.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a targeted penalty increase, not a rewrite of robocall rules. Its benefit is a stronger deterrent against large-scale scam operations, which cost consumers billions annually; its cost is modest and falls almost entirely on violators. The main limitation is that it only works if prosecutors use it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on December 4, 2025, and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no further action; Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto introduced the DO NOT Call Act on December 4, 2025, joined by Sens. Klobuchar, Gillibrand, and King [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S4].
No further action has been taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has won or lost much: the bill has simply not moved. Robocall operations and telemarketers continue operating under existing civil-only penalties, while consumers continue receiving illegal calls at today's rates. The four sponsoring senators can point to an introduced bill without having secured a hearing or vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; status quo holds

sides.party_line_note: Only four senators are attached — three Democrats and one independent — with no Republican cosponsors and no votes taken, so the partisan shape of the bill is not yet visible.

industries.note: The bill would expose willful TCPA violators to up to three years in prison and double spoofing fines from $10,000 to $20,000. Legitimate consent-based telemarketers are largely unaffected; the burden falls on operators that break the rules at scale [S2].

Scam robocalls are the bill's clearest target: operations using autodialers to further felonies or costing victims $5,000 or more would face felony-level penalties, and fake caller ID would cost twice as much per violation [S2].

The 'call' definition expressly includes autodialed texts, widening the conduct covered, but liability attaches to the party who initiates illegal calls, not to carriers or platforms that merely transmit them.

analysis.trajectory: With four sponsors, no Republican support, no committee action more than a year before Congress ends, and no companion House bill in the record, the bill's likely path is to sit in the Commerce Committee and die at the end of the Congress, as most referred Senate bills do.
